fa: William Degenhardt & Herbert (H.V.) Strandberg, 1932 (Seattle Mountaineers) — the peak's original line, climbed the summer after the pair first glimpsed the Southern Pickets in 1931
overview: Officially "Pinnacle Peak" on USGS maps, but almost universally called The Chopping Block for its distinctive squarish, blocky summit block. It sits at the south end of the Barrier Ridge in the Southern Pickets, North Cascades National Park, dividing Terror Creek Basin from Crescent Creek Basin, and is visible from the Newhalem visitor center on clear days. First climbed in 1932 by Bill Degenhardt and H. V. Strandberg — their summit cairn reportedly remained undisturbed for decades — it's now a
beta: Climbers approach via Goodell Creek and Terror Creek to a high camp on the Stump Hollow ridge below the peak, then climb 3rd/4th class terrain with a short section of low-5th-class rock (5.4) to reach the summit. Because the Pickets guard several summits from a shared basin, parties frequently combine this peak with Mount Degenhardt, Mount Terror, or Inspiration Peak on the same trip.

first_pass.evidence: South-side party: 'a couple of short, exposed sections that might have been low fifth class'; Wikipedia lists easiest route as YDS 5 with no number.
first_pass.note: No source gives a number; the record's 5.5 headline and 5.4 breakdown are both unsupported. Low 5th with no number -> 5.0 per brief.

rock_grade: 3rd-4th class with a few moves of low 5th (unrated)
fa: Don Gordon, 1951 (first ascent of the peak)
overview: The Pyramid is a compact, seldom-visited summit on the crest of the Southern Pickets, set on the ridge between Mount Degenhardt to the west and Inspiration Peak to the east. At roughly 7,920 ft it is the shortest of the range's named summits, overshadowed by its 8,000-ft-plus neighbors, and is almost never climbed as a stand-alone objective -- nearly every ascent happens as one stop within a longer traverse of the range. Despite looking broken and unpromising from a distance, parties who've clim
beta: From a high camp near the Terror Glacier or in Crescent Creek Basin, parties cross The Barrier (the connecting ridge between Terror and Crescent Creek basins) and work across broken, sometimes loose terrain toward the notch south of Mount Degenhardt, then traverse east along the connecting ridge onto Pyramid's west side. The line climbs a gully/couloir system on scrambling terrain with a few low fifth-class moves; staying left in the gully rather than attempting the overhanging rock directly abo

first_pass.evidence: Trip report: from Degenhardt, 3rd-4th class with a few moves of low 5th to leave the ridge onto Pyramid; no number anywhere.

overview: The middle of the three summits and the harder of the trio to reach, Middle Peak is typically climbed from a glacier camp near the col between it and the North Peak rather than as a standalone 'south face' outing — most parties combine it with the North Peak in a two- or three-summit push. It sees far less traffic than the ladder-and-lookout South Peak.
beta: The Middle Peak is climbed far less often than the South Peak (lookout) or North Peak and has very little published route detail; it shares the same long Goat Flats/Tin Can Gap approach as the other two summits before diverging toward the Middle Peak's south side. Treat any attempt as a serious, lightly-documented alpine rock objective and be prepared to route-find.

first_pass.evidence: Little route-specific beta; Middle Finger described as the hardest-looking of the three, with class 4 scrambling reported.
first_pass.note: rock_grade says 'low fifth class' but breakdown tops at Class 3-4; no source settles it.

route: West Peak via West Ridge - West Face
overview: A rock scramble/climb up Three Queens' West Peak (6,400 ft) via its West Ridge and West Face, approached from a high camp at Spectacle Point after a multi-day hike in via Mineral Creek and Park Lakes.
beta: After camping at Spectacle Point (5,800 ft), the route climbs the West Ridge and West Face of West Peak to the summit — a mix of rock scrambling and rock climbing, i.e. class 3-4 terrain without a documented technical crux comparable to the Middle Peak chimney.
breakdown: Spectacle Point camp to West Peak summit: Class 3-4 scramble/climb

first_pass.evidence: SummitPost: West Tower is the hardest summit (class 5); trip report: easiest routes on Main/Middle/West are Class 3/4/5, West Queen's final pitch 'Class 5.7ish' on questionable rock with sketchy pro.
first_pass.note: Record's breakdown says Class 3-4; sources say the West Peak is 5th class.

peak: Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower
overview: A relatively obscure, rarely-repeated 600-foot class 5 granite line up Thunder Mountain's north face, above the Thunder Mountain Lakes basin, first climbed in 1972 — in contrast to the standard 3rd-class scramble route to the same 6,556 ft summit via the SE slopes.
beta: The north face is 600 feet of class 5 granite climbing, first ascended by Bruce Garrett and Dennis Nelson on July 6, 1972. Little further pitch-by-pitch or modern beta exists for this specific line; it sees far less traffic than the popular SE-slope scramble or the nearby Slippery Slab Tower climb.
breakdown: Full route: 5th class (specific YDS grade not documented)

first_pass.evidence: SummitPost: north face is granite with 600 ft of class 5, first climbed 1972; no YDS number published.

rock_grade: Class 4-5 (low 5th class scrambling; no specific YDS number grade attested)
fa: Everett and Ida Darr, 1940 (first ascent of the peak)
overview: Tupshin Peak (8,347 ft) is one of the 'Stehekin Seven,' a knot of rarely visited summits above the Stehekin valley in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. The mountain is built of several rock turrets running south, east, and northwest from a central high point roughly 200 ft above its neighbors. First climbed in 1940 by Everett and Ida Darr, it's approached entirely by boat and trail (no road reaches the peak). The standard line climbs the broad south ridge/upper east face to a short, exposed, and nota
beta: From Bird Creek Camp, climb NNE up open sub-alpine slope to a broad shoulder (~7,000 ft) on Tupshin's lower South Ridge, then traverse/descend slightly around cliff bands into the upper east basin (~7,500 ft) below the face — about one mile from Bird Creek to the base of the climbing. The basin is a talus fan, often snow-covered early season. From there, rambly Class 2-4 terrain and a short crux (5.2-5.4, on a flake/crack) lead through the face to Class 3-4 summit-pyramid scrambling and the top.
breakdown: Basin to base of face: Class 2 (snow)

first_pass.evidence: Southeast-face standard: Class 4 with a few Class 5 moves; one report names a 4th-class chimney to a 5.4 crux, often rappelled.

face: South slope to the south side of the summit block, right of the Classic Route
overview: An easy, low-angle alternative up wide left-leaning cracks to the right of the Classic Route's base, sharing summit anchors with The Roof.
beta: Starts at two wide, left-leaning cracks about 50 ft right of the base of the Classic Route; climbs up and left toward the shared anchors (block with tat and rings) used by The Roof.

first_pass.evidence: MP: Open Book rated 'Easy 5th' (no number), left-leaning cracks east of The Roof.
first_pass.note: Easy 5th with no number anywhere -> 5.0 per brief.

peak: Upper Black Ice and Winter Ice Crag

first_pass.evidence: No route of this name found; carries the identical 'WI4 M4' grade of CYA at the same crag.

fa: Fred Berry and Lawrence Buchanan, 1936 (first ascent of the peak)
overview: Whatcom Peak stands guard at the northwest gateway to the Picket Range above Whatcom Pass, one of the more accessible summits in a range known for brutal approaches. This Southwest/Whatcom Glacier line is the standard way to combine Whatcom Peak with neighboring Mount Challenger. Like most Picket Range glaciers, the Whatcom Glacier has thinned noticeably in recent years — parties recently describe sections of bare ice and a badly deteriorated summit notch by late summer, so do not assume conditi
beta: From Whatcom Pass the standard approach descends on a traversing line to about 5,200 ft to round the base of Whatcom Peak's NW rib, then crosses polished slabs below the Whatcom Glacier on the peak's east side to reach Perfect Pass at the south side of the mountain. From Perfect Pass the summit is 'an easy grab' — a snow slope of moderate angle followed by a short but exposed Class 3 ridge scramble to the higher, northeast summit point. The Whatcom Glacier is shrinking quickly and can present ba
breakdown: Whatcom Pass to glacier traverse: Class 2, glacier

first_pass.evidence: South-side routes from Perfect Pass/Whatcom Glacier: snowfields then 3rd class rock to the summit; no separate grade found for a 'Southwest Route'.

overview: A serious snow-and-ice ascent of the Northwest Shoulder, following the same Lone Tree Pass/High Pass line as the standard route but climbed while the couloir and So-Bahli-Ahli (Whitehorse) Glacier are still consolidated snow rather than open crevasse and bare-ice terrain. Sustained steep snow/glacier travel gives way to a firm summit block (up to roughly 50°) and a short Class 3-4 rock finish. This line is also the standard ski/splitboard descent off the peak.
beta: Follows the same lower approach as the standard Northwest Shoulder (Niederprum Trail to Lone Tree Pass), but from the Whitehorse Ridge/Ashton Creek drainage stays on the glacier proper (climber's right to avoid the worst crevassing), ascends a steep icy rollover around 5,600 ft, then climbs the So-Bahli-Ahli Glacier toward a firm, icy summit block finished with Class 3-4 scrambling.
breakdown: Approach to Whitehorse Ridge / glacier edge: Class 2, brushy/snow
So-Bahli-Ahli Glacier to summit block: Glacier + Class 3-4

first_pass.evidence: Same NW Shoulder line; steep snow/ice to ~50-55 degrees and Class 3-4 summit rock (later season); no published ice grade found.
first_pass.note: AI2 in ice_grade is not supported by any source seen; steep snow mapped by the brief would be Class 3, rock top is Class 4.
